title: Inconsistent AI restrictions on GameBanana are undermining transparency and accessibility in modding
author: Elegant_Attempt2790
selftext:
i recently had a [Deadlock cosmetic mod](https://gamebanana.com/mods/744392) removed from GameBanana after voluntarily disclosing my use of coding agents during development. i work alongside them, writing, reviewing and debugging code myself while also delegating implementation, research and testing

looking into the policy, i found some discrepancies with implications well beyond my own mod. communities can set boundaries on AI usage, but at minimum, those boundaries should be clearly defined and consistently enforced

## GameBanana, according to GameBanana

in June 2026, Deadlock’s game managers held a [poll](https://gamebanana.com/polls/5006) on banning most AI content. 86% voted in favour (367–58), with the proposed rule including a limited exception for assisted coding

the current [R-DL.847](https://gamebanana.com/games/rules/20948#GameRule.847) prohibits generated content, including “vibe code”:

> with the sole exception of AI assisted coding, which requires them to follow the site rules.

its fix instructions reiterate:

> Properly disclose AI assisted code in your submission page as written in the Site Rules.

[one modding tool](https://gamebanana.com/tools/23606) received a softhold requesting a missing AI disclaimer. meanwhile, [other removal notices](https://gamebanana.com/mods/726112) describe the restriction as follows:

> AI Assisting, or Generating throughout the entire modding process is not allowed.

[recent removals](https://gamebanana.com/mods/745790) repeat this position

so which is it?

GameBanana’s [site-wide AI policy](https://gamebanana.com/wikis/2175), section 5.5, explicitly defines AI assistance as including:

> Writing individual lines, functions, or entire blocks of code.

it also includes debugging, refactoring and restructuring, regardless of how extensive the assistance was. indirect use for explanations and general information doesn’t require disclosure when it doesn’t directly contribute to the submitted code

their Human Contribution Requirement recognizes substantial refinement and integration as meaningful human involvement, prohibits uncritically submitting generated work, and explicitly states that its purpose is not to:

> impose arbitrary limits on how much of a project may be AI-generated.

developers remain responsible for reviewing their work, licensing, attribution and accurate disclosure. all fairly reasonable requirements imo

i’d favour assessing meaningful human involvement over whether individual implementations were delegated. if Deadlock intends to apply a narrower definition of assisted coding, what is it? does it extend to internal development tooling that isn’t even distributed with the mod?

[one developer](https://gamebanana.com/threads/229437) reports three removals, including a mod composed entirely of existing Valve models that reportedly used AI-assisted tooling. [another](https://gamebanana.com/members/5512678) voluntarily removed several mods over LLM-assisted rigging tasks and intends to maintain them elsewhere

i’ve contacted GameBanana for clarification on how these restrictions fit its [guidance for game managers](https://gamebanana.com/wikis/2012). regardless of how much autonomy individual game sections have, the community voted on a rule with an exception. communicating and enforcing that exception consistently seems like a reasonable starting point

## who exactly are we protecting?

personally, i don’t particularly want to see AI-generated artwork when browsing for mods either. i’d appreciate being able to filter it out without also excluding someone whose development pipeline involves coding agents

if two developers produce identical assets through different technical workflows, how reliably can moderators distinguish between them? what happens when voluntary disclosure becomes the primary evidence used to remove a submission?

[Nexus Mods](https://www.nexusmods.com/news/15654) addressed this in its November 3 policy announcement:

> An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use.

a [2025 PNAS paper](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2426766122), comprising four preregistered experiments with 4,439 participants, documented negative evaluations of AI users’ competence and motivation. participants in one experiment also expressed less willingness to disclose their AI use

workplace behaviour isn’t modding, but if you actively want to avoid AI-generated content, how does giving developers another reason not to disclose it benefit you?

during the original Deadlock poll, an account carrying GameBanana’s owner rank, “End Boss”, actually proposed a draft policy with filterable AI usage scores, acknowledging that:

> almost everything is going to contain some AI-assistance somewhere in its development process.

GameBanana has since introduced its [AI Usage module](https://gamebanana.com/blogs/22155), requiring separate disclosures for art, code, audio, design and submission elements. its announcement explicitly mentions plans for list filters

category-specific filters would let consumers distinguish generated artwork from programming assistance. they wouldn’t resolve training-data objections or eliminate social stigma, but permitting properly disclosed assistance would remove one incentive to conceal it

consumer choice is only one side of this discussion, though. what about access to creating in the first place?

one of GameBanana’s [four core philosophies](https://gamebanana.com/wikis/1931) is:

> To always be non-elitist. We respect all submitters and artists, regardless of skill level.

i think part of welcoming new talent is considering the barriers people face when learning and creating in the first place

a [2024 ASSETS paper](https://research.google/pubs/painting-with-cameras-and-drawing-with-text-exploring-responsible-ai-and-greater-design-for-accessible-creativity/) interviewed ten disabled creatives, including people who intentionally use and avoid generative AI. despite their differing perspectives, the authors raise questions about whose creative practices are overlooked in efforts to protect artists

there’s research concerning programming, too:

- [ASSETS 2022](https://doi.org/10.1145/3517428.3550392): motor-impaired programmers struggled with conventional speech recognition, including memorizing unnatural commands. five of seven wanted natural language programming capabilities
- [CHI 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16491): visually impaired developers reported benefits from AI coding assistants alongside new accessibility challenges
- [CHI 2026](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790726): a two-week study of sixteen blind and low-vision programmers documented accessibility benefits alongside verification and control difficulties. one participant previously focused on backend development used AI to assist with interface development, reviewing and refining the code themselves

personally, as someone with aphantasia, being able to externalize ideas is incredibly valuable. similar benefits have been documented in [accessibility research from 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.09924)

these papers don’t suggest every application of AI should be permitted. they do suggest accessibility deserves consideration when deciding which applications to restrict

what happens when someone relies on tools that fall outside the coding exception, or when that exception itself is inconsistently enforced?

**would someone be expected to disclose personal medical information to justify their choice of development tools?**

i’d rather see clearly defined permissions for activities like research, internal tooling and coding assistance than leave volunteers to determine whose disability warrants an exception

i understand wanting to protect artists. i’d just like disabled artists and developers to be included in that conversation

## what are we actually trying to prevent?

if the concern is training data, let’s discuss consent, licensing and attribution. if it’s preserving manual craftsmanship, let’s be explicit about that objective and who it excludes

neither is the same as addressing spam or inadequate testing

GameBanana’s [moderation guidance](https://gamebanana.com/wikis/2014) already addresses deliberately low-quality submissions while explicitly stating:

> Beginner content is allowed

if someone uploads 20 pieces of spam, moderate the spam. if someone uploads 30 genuinely good mods, why are we displaying 30 consecutive listings from one developer? show a couple, group the rest and give users the option to see more

GameBanana already regulates excessive [submission updates](https://gamebanana.com/wikis/1957) because they affect discovery. [Nexus Mods](https://www.nexusmods.com/news/15654) is exploring author-level visibility limits and tighter restrictions on new accounts

i appreciate that volunteers have limited resources. a blanket ban might be easier to apply when someone discloses their workflow, but that doesn’t make undisclosed use any easier to identify

maintainability, technical understanding and skill-sharing matter. why not encourage documentation, testing and compatibility information directly, rather than infer those qualities from someone’s choice of tools?

other GameBanana communities already offer examples:

- [Friday Night Funkin’](https://gamebanana.com/mods/710660) exempts assisted code and text-to-speech while retaining spam and low-effort restrictions
- [WorldBox](https://gamebanana.com/mods/723938) enforces additional disclosure requirements
- [Tears of the Kingdom](https://gamebanana.com/blogs/22441) has guidance covering AI attribution, authentic gameplay screenshots, compatibility and testing

even [Modrinth](https://support.modrinth.com/en/articles/16551575-disclosure-and-usage-of-ai), which explicitly cites ethical, economic and ecological objections to AI, distinguishes substantial generated contributions from things like code review and minor refactoring

Valve itself states in its [Steamworks documentation](https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/contentsurvey):

> Efficiency gains through the use of these tools is not the focus of this section.

Steam and GameBanana serve different purposes, but distinguishing development assistance from generated material distributed to players seems useful in both contexts

---

i genuinely think a lot of the Deadlock community wants to protect artists and maintain a healthy modding scene. i just think some of these restrictions risk undermining those intentions

at minimum, clarify and consistently enforce the existing coding exception. beyond that, improve discovery, follow through on filtering plans and consider accessibility when developing these policies

perhaps my favourite find was GameBanana’s moderation documentation under [Discretion](https://gamebanana.com/wikis/2047):

> We have rules, but ultimately rules come second to discretion.

it warns about the damage blindly enforcing rules can do to a modding community and GameBanana’s reputation. the stated purpose of moderation is to:

> facilitate and foster modding and creativity.

i’d quite like to see the Deadlock section held to that standard

i’d be interested in how other developers and community managers are approaching disclosure, accessibility and the distinction between development assistance and generated content within their own communities

you cannot reasonably expect a community to uphold transparency while simultaneously making transparency a liability for developers

- [An Autoethnographic Case Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence’s Utility for Accessibility (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.09924)

comments.author: Ohgood9002
comments.body: No one cares. Complain on the deadlock boards, not here

I made an extensive mod for Lego City Undercover that I published the other day. Massive overhaul of the game. I've been a software engineer for 12+ years and I disclosed that I'd used AI in the GitHub repo. This is my first mod. 

However, I'm not part of any modding community and only posted it to reddit. My mod is completely standalone and I have no intentions to integrate it with their modding system. 

For some reason I've been getting a bunch of hate from people in the LCU modding community, as if I'm taking something away from their work. DMs and comments on my post. The worst stuff is in the DMs. It's just baffling.

replies.author: torpidcerulean
replies.body: A big part of modding communities is the reputation and insularity; it's like how media fandoms have their insider rules and expectations that often expand far beyond the original text. You're a no name to them, releasing your first mod, using AI. I'm sure you made the big names in the LCU modding community very upset about "stolen valor."

replies.author: MelodramaticShape
replies.body:
I made an extremely popular mod with several hundred thousand downloads. I pulled the plug on it because of some really entitled and obnoxious people within the game's community. Same thing that you're talking about. Ultimately they got what they wanted. Never doing that again, fuck those guys I sincerely hope they live miserable lives.   
  
tl;dr - Make your own thing. It's more rewarding and you don't have to answer to anyone.

Yeah it's a significant breakthrough in what is possible in modding this 13 year old game. I made it for me and my kid and just randomly decided to share it so I'm really not worried at all. I'm going to keep updating it and sharing it. The funny thing it's all open source. They can take it and use it as they please.
